name: Anthracnose leaf spot
summary: A laboratory-confirmed Cannabis leaf-spot disease caused by Colletotrichum fioriniae. A Kentucky first report established a light-green-speck to tan-centered, dark-margined lesion sequence and fulfilled pathogenicity testing, while a later university survey only corroborated separate field occurrences. Photographs cannot distinguish it from other leaf-spot pathogens or physical injury.
affectedParts: adjacent leaf tissue when lesions coalesce
both leaf surfaces for paired documentation
stages: field-grown reproductive hemp in the first report
indicators: The reported sequence began with scattered light-green specks rather than an immediately open hole.
Developing lesions became round or angular and approximately 3 to 4 mm across.
Compatible lesions had tan centers, darker brown margins, and yellow halos, but this color combination is not unique to anthracnose.
Lesion centers could crack and later drop out, creating a shot-hole or frog-eye appearance only after surrounding lesion development.
Multiple lesions could coalesce into larger necrotic regions rather than remaining isolated dots.
Lesions reaching a margin could be associated with marginal scorching, puckering, or twisting.
A useful image set pairs the full leaf and plant context with calibrated close views of intact early, developing, and center-loss lesions.
Compatible C. fioriniae culture morphology plus multilocus sequence evidence from the same lesion substantially strengthens the label; visual morphology alone does not.
exclusions: Physical holes, chewing, hail tears, handling damage, or training injury occur without a preceding discolored lesion, halo, or lesion-linked fungus.
Dark embedded pycnidia and a compatible laboratory result support Septoria leaf spot.
Gray-brown sooty or velvety lower-surface conidial patches support Pseudocercospora.
Tan-to-white centers with conspicuous melanized conidiophores and a compatible result support Cercospora leaf spot.
Concentric target-like rings or dark central sporulation with a compatible isolate support Alternaria as a differential.
Angular water-soaked lesions, bacterial streaming or ooze, and a plant-linked bacterial identification support bacterial leaf spot.
A sharp spray, lamp, aisle, contact, or weather boundary without lesion-linked Colletotrichum evidence supports abiotic injury.
Culture, microscopy, multilocus sequencing, or repeated representative sampling identifies another organism or fails to link C. fioriniae to the lesions.

progression.description: Capture symptom-free leaves and plant position before or beside the affected cohort whenever matched controls are available.
Scattered light-green specks appear while tissue remains intact; record leaf age, canopy position, both surfaces, and field distribution.
Specks develop into approximately 3 to 4 mm round or angular lesions with tan centers, darker margins, and yellow halos.
Necrotic centers crack and may drop out; follow the same tagged lesion so an insect or mechanical hole is not mistaken for progression.
Lesions merge into larger necrotic areas, and marginal involvement may accompany scorching, puckering, or twisting.

lookAlikes: Four-lined plant bug or other puncture injury
Caterpillar, beetle, slug, or snail feeding
Hail, wind, handling, or training tear
Edema or localized water-related tissue collapse
confirmation: Photograph the entire plant and canopy neighborhood, then both surfaces of several affected and unaffected leaves with a scale and stable plant identifiers.
Track the same intact early lesions through center cracking or loss; a single frame of an existing hole cannot establish the reported progression.
Collect multiple fresh lesions spanning intact early margins to developing centers before saprophytes obscure the lesion edge, following the receiving laboratory's packaging instructions.
Use lesion-edge culture and trained morphological examination to recover a dominant compatible Colletotrichum isolate, while recording other organisms recovered from the same tissue.

For C. fioriniae-level confirmation, require plant-linked multilocus sequence evidence comparable to the four-gene approach in the first report; do not assign the species from color, ITS alone, or a generic Colletotrichum image.
Where causality is uncertain or the isolate represents a new host or presentation, use pathogenicity evidence with symptom reproduction, reisolation, and symptomless controls.

Keep symptom-only, shot-hole-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, single-locus-only, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, unverified, and low-resolution samples out of confirmed training labels and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Tag and photograph representative plants before removing tissue, preserving the spatial pattern and lesion sequence.
Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and retain traceable fresh samples for a plant diagnostic laboratory.
Map affected plants against cultivar blocks, irrigation or splash zones, airflow, recent foliar applications, handling paths, and weather injury.
correctivePlan: Base disease management on the organism confirmed by the diagnostic laboratory and the production setting rather than on the anthracnose name or a photograph alone.
Contain or remove confirmed diseased material as locally appropriate and follow new lesion incidence on tagged plants; old necrotic tissue will not recover.
Reassess the diagnosis if new lesions do not follow the documented sequence or if repeated plant-linked tests do not support C. fioriniae.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic leaves, debris, tools, or splash water into clean production areas.
Reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness and retain adequate spacing and airflow where feasible.
Scout with stable plant IDs and matched full-plant, full-leaf, and macro views so early specks can be distinguished from later center loss.
warnings: Shot-hole, frog-eye, tan-center, dark-margin, yellow-halo, puckering, and coalescence features are not individually or jointly species-specific in a photograph.

The first report is a narrow Kentucky report; it does not establish national prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, universal canopy or leaf-age preference, infection timing, yield loss, or action thresholds.
The 2021 Kentucky survey only reports separate field occurrences and explicitly characterizes its findings as preliminary; it does not validate a camera-only label.
A Colletotrichum culture without plant and lesion linkage can represent incidental or secondary recovery and is not sufficient ground truth.
No image or video was indexed because no stable, item-level Cannabis anthracnose asset with clear reuse rights, plant linkage, and species-resolved confirmation was verified.
All symptom-only, hole-only, detached, mixed-organism, unlinked-laboratory, single-locus-only, low-resolution, and rights-unclear samples require human review.

sources.title: First Report of Anthracnose Leaf Spot Caused by Colletotrichum fioriniae on Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: Hemp anthracnose lesions began as light-green specks and developed into 3 to 4 mm round or angular spots with tan centers, darker brown margins, and yellow halos; centers could crack or drop out and lesions could coalesce.
Colletotrichum fioriniae was identified by morphology and four gene sequences, and inoculation reproduced characteristic leaf spots while controls remained symptomless.
Shot-hole or frog-eye appearance is not species-specific and must be differentiated from other fungal and bacterial leaf spots.

sources.title: Observations of Insect and Disease Pests on Field Grown Hemp in Kentucky
sources.organization: Science of Hemp: Production and Pest Management Conference Proceedings
sources.publisher: Auburn University College of Agriculture and Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station
supportedClaims: A 2021 University of Kentucky survey at the Spindletop Farm and Robinson Center observed separate cases of anthracnose identified as Colletotrichum fioriniae in field-grown hemp research plantings.

The survey covered hemp grown for cannabinoid, grain, and fiber purposes and documented multiple fungal diseases in the same season, so field context does not make a photographed lesion specific to anthracnose.

The conference report explicitly described its results as preliminary and called for additional research; it does not establish prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, symptom timing, yield impact, or a visual decision threshold for anthracnose.
